scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

prediction.raw: 1. In this scenario, the parents are wrong for insisting that the therapist disclose the reason why their son wants to see him. The therapist has a professional obligation to maintain confidentiality, which is a fundamental principle in the therapeutic relationship. This means that the therapist cannot disclose any information about the sessions without the client's (in this case, the son's) consent. The parents' insistence on knowing the reason why their son wants to see a therapist is understandable, given their concern for their child's well-being. However, their approach is misguided. By pushing the therapist to disclose confidential information, they are potentially undermining the therapeutic relationship and creating a sense of mistrust between their son and the therapist. The son's reaction, feeling insulted and not talking to his parents, suggests that he feels his trust has been violated. This is a common issue in therapy, where clients may not want to disclose certain information to their parents or guardians, and it's essential to respect their boundaries. The parents should respect their son's autonomy and the therapist's professional boundaries. Instead of insisting on knowing the reason, they could try having an open and non-judgmental conversation with their son, letting him know that they are there to support him and that they care about his well-being. This approach would help build trust and create a safe space for their son to open up about his feelings and concerns.
